summary.text: Gauss's law is one of Maxwell's equations; it ties the distribution of electric charge to the electric field that the charge produces.
It says the flux of the electric field out of any closed surface is proportional to the charge enclosed, however that charge is spread out.
The law alone cannot fix the field everywhere, but where a problem has spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry it makes the field easy to find.

facts.label: First formulated
facts.value: By Lagrange in 1773, then Gauss in 1835

facts.label: Flux and charge
facts.value: Net flux equals enclosed charge times 1/ε₀

facts.label: Close relatives
facts.value: Matching laws exist for magnetism and for gravity

items.prompt: An imaginary closed surface is drawn around a group of charges. What decides the net electric flux out through it?

options.label: The total charge inside, however it is arranged
How close the nearest charge sits to the wall
Only the shape and size of the surface itself
The charges lying outside the surface

items.explain: The flux out of a closed surface is proportional to the charge it encloses, irrespective of how that charge is distributed.

items.prompt: A ball of charge is spread evenly through a sphere. Why does the law make the field outside easy to find?

options.label: Round objects have no electric field
The charge can be treated as zero
The symmetry makes the field uniform across a surface
Spheres cancel all flux that passes through them

items.explain: The total flux alone says little about the field, but symmetry forces the field through the surface to be uniform, so it can be deduced at every point.

items.prompt: One person must find a conductor's charge from a measured field. Another must find the field from a known charge layout that has no symmetry. Who has the harder job?

options.label: The first, because charge hides inside the metal
Neither, since the law makes both equally easy
The first, because no tools exist for it
The second, because total flux says little about the field

items.explain: Finding charge from the field is possible through the flux through a small box; the reverse is much more difficult without symmetry.

items.prompt: Why is Gauss's law regarded as more general than Coulomb's law?

options.label: It works for stationary charges only
It holds for moving charges too
It ignores the superposition principle
It applies only to charges at rest in a vacuum

items.explain: Coulomb's law applies only to stationary charges, while Gauss's law holds for moving charges as well.

items.prompt: The charge sitting on a capacitor plate, or moved around by static electricity, is classed as which kind?

options.label: Free charge
Bound charge
Magnetic charge
Virtual charge

items.explain: Free charge covers the simplest textbook cases like static electricity and capacitor plates; bound charge arises only in polarizable materials.

items.prompt: Gravity weakens with the square of distance. Which law is Gauss's law for gravity essentially equivalent to?

options.label: Ohm's law
Snell's law
Newton's law of gravity
Faraday's law

items.explain: Any inverse-square law can be written in a Gauss-like form; Gauss's law for gravity is essentially equivalent to Newton's law of gravity.

paragraphs.heading: What the law says
paragraphs.text: Gauss's law is one of Maxwell's equations, the set that underpins classical electrodynamics. It connects the way electric charge is spread out with the electric field that charge produces. It also goes by the name Gauss's flux theorem.

paragraphs.heading: Flux through a closed surface
paragraphs.text: Picture any imaginary closed surface drawn around some charges; it is called a Gaussian surface. The electric flux is the electric field added up over that whole surface. The law says the net flux coming out equals the charge inside multiplied by 1/ε₀. It does not matter how that charge is arranged inside the surface.

paragraphs.heading: When symmetry helps
paragraphs.text: On its own, the total flux usually says little about the field, which can weave in and out of the surface in tangled patterns. But some problems have a symmetry that forces the field to cross the surface evenly. Then, once the total flux is known, the field can be worked out at every point. Spherical, cylindrical and planar symmetry are the usual cases.

paragraphs.heading: Two forms of one law
paragraphs.text: The version with flux over a surface is called the integral form. The differential form works point by point: it says the divergence of the field at a place is proportional to the charge per unit volume there. The two forms are mathematically the same, tied together by the divergence theorem. Each can also be written with the electric field E and all the charge, or with the displacement field D and the free charge only.

paragraphs.heading: Free and bound charge
paragraphs.text: Free charge is the kind met in simple cases, such as static electricity or the charge on a capacitor plate. Bound charge appears in materials that can be polarized: in an outside field, their electrons stay with their atoms but shift a tiny distance to one side. All those tiny shifts add up to a net spread of charge at large scale. There are often practical reasons to treat this bound charge separately, which is why the D form uses free charge alone.

paragraphs.heading: A cousin of Coulomb's law
paragraphs.text: Gauss's law and Coulomb's law can each be derived from the other. Neither follows from the other alone: getting Gauss's law from Coulomb's needs the superposition principle, the idea that the total field is the vector sum of the fields from each particle. Coulomb's law covers only charges at rest, yet Gauss's law holds for moving charges too. In that respect Gauss's law is the more general of the two.

paragraphs.heading: History and relatives
paragraphs.text: Joseph-Louis Lagrange first stated the law in 1773, and Carl Friedrich Gauss followed in 1835; both were studying how ellipsoids attract. Matching laws exist for magnetism and for gravity. In fact any inverse-square law can be written in the same shape, and Gauss's law for gravity is essentially Newton's law of gravity in another dress.
